values.value: Notes on the Model Context Protocol and why it changes how we work with tools like Umbraco.

Field notes on the Model Context Protocol: the small open standard that lets AI assistants plug into the tools you already use. This whole site was modelled, written and published through Umbraco's MCP server.

value.markup:
Welcome

Every page you are reading, from the document types and block grids behind it to the images and the words themselves, was created by an AI agent talking to Umbraco through the Model Context Protocol. No clicking around the backoffice, no import scripts. Below are a couple of posts on why that is a bigger deal than it sounds.

values.value: MCP is the USB-C port for AI
Why one open protocol beats a thousand bespoke integrations, and what that means for AI assistants.
Before USB, every device had its own plug. Before MCP, every AI integration had its own glue code. Here's why one open protocol beats a thousand bespoke connectors.

value.markup:
Dig through a drawer of old electronics and you'll find the history of connectors: barrel plugs, proprietary docks, mini-USB, micro-USB, and a dozen chargers that fit exactly one thing each. Every new device meant a new cable. USB-C didn't make devices smarter. It made them interchangeable.

AI assistants have had the same drawer problem. Want your model to read a database, open a ticket, or edit a web page? Someone had to write a custom integration for that specific model and that specific tool. With M models and N tools you end up maintaining M × N pieces of glue code, and every one of them breaks in its own way.

One plug, both directions

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that turns that M × N problem into M + N. A tool vendor writes one MCP server describing what their system can do. An AI application implements one MCP client. Any client can then talk to any server. Build once, connect everywhere.

values.value: A bundle of cables, one integration each. Photo: Lucian Alexe on Unsplash.

value.markup:
What a server actually offers

An MCP server describes its capabilities in a way a model can discover at runtime. There are three main building blocks:

  • Tools: actions the model can take, such as create a document, run a query or upload an image. Each one has a name, a description and a JSON schema for its inputs.
  • Resources: read-only context the model can pull in, like files, records or API responses.
  • Prompts: reusable templates a server can offer for common tasks.

Because the schema travels with the tool, the model doesn't need to be trained on your API. It reads the description, works out the shape of the input and makes the call. Add a new tool to the server and every connected assistant can use it immediately.

values.value: USB-C didn't make devices smarter. It made them interchangeable. MCP does the same for AI and the tools it works with.

value.markup:
Why open matters

Plenty of platforms have had plugin systems before. The difference is that MCP isn't owned by any one assistant. It's an open specification built on plain JSON-RPC, and it runs over standard transports: a local process talking over stdio, or a remote service over HTTP. That makes it cheap to adopt and safe to bet on. The server you write today works with the assistant you switch to tomorrow.

It also keeps you in control. The server decides which tools exist and what credentials they run with. The client decides when to ask a human for permission. The model never gets more access than the server explicitly hands it.

The takeaway

MCP is boring in the best possible way. It's a plug. And once everything shares the same plug, the interesting work moves from writing glue code to deciding what you actually want your tools to do.

values.value: Your CMS, now with a conversation
What happens when an AI agent can model, write and publish in Umbraco through MCP. This blog is the demo.
This blog was built by an AI agent working through Umbraco's MCP server: content model, media, posts and all. Here's what that looks like, and why it's more than a party trick.

value.markup:
The usual way to stand up a site in a CMS is a long afternoon of clicking: create a document type, add properties, configure a block grid, upload images, write content, publish, repeat. It's not hard work, but it's a lot of it.

The site you're reading took a different route. An AI agent was given a short brief ("a blog with a front page and two posts, built with blocks") and access to Umbraco's MCP server. Everything else happened through tool calls.

What the agent actually did

  1. Modelled the content. It created element types for a hero, rich text, images, quotes and a post list, then filed them into the project's Blocks folder. It created an SEO composition and two page types, and wired them together with block grid data types.
  2. Imported media. It pulled photos from a local folder into the media library, inside a folder as the house rules require.
  3. Wrote and published content. The front page and both posts were created as structured block grid JSON, read back to verify, then published.

values.value: Less clicking, more deciding. Photo: Christopher Gower on Unsplash.

value.markup:
It follows the rules

The interesting part isn't speed. It's that the agent works inside the CMS's own model. It uses the same document types, data types and validation an editor would. Nothing gets bolted on from outside, so nothing gets out of sync.

Because the project's conventions are written down (where each kind of type lives, how aliases are named, how blocks render), the agent can follow them just like a new team member would. It does it on the first try, every time.

values.value: The point isn't that the machine clicks faster. It's that the CMS becomes something you can talk to.

value.markup:
Where this goes next

Scaffolding a demo blog is the easy case. The same tools cover the jobs that eat real editorial time: restructuring a content model across hundreds of pages, migrating copy from an old site, auditing every page for a missing meta description, or translating a section into a new language. These tasks are tedious for people and easy to describe to an agent.

And because it's MCP, none of it is tied to a single assistant. Any MCP client can drive the same server, with the same permissions, against the same management API your backoffice already uses.

So: MCP is awesome. Not because it's magic, but because it gives your existing tools a front door that AI can walk through, without anyone having to build a new house.
